---
title: "Client-side and Server-side Load Balancing"
description: "A worked microservices lesson using the shop-services example."
---

**Course source:** Day 1 §6–7. **Running system:** Order, Product, and User services.

## Product now has two instances

Order may send a request to Product A or Product B. We need an instance-selection policy. The course compares **client-side** and **server-side** load balancing.

~~~text
Client-side: Order -> choose A or B -> Product instance
Server-side: Order -> Stable Proxy -> choose A or B
~~~

With client-side balancing, Order uses a registry's instance list and applies a rule locally. With server-side balancing, a gateway, service or proxy makes the selection; Order can use one stable destination name.

## Compare the trade-offs

A client-side strategy avoids a central request-processing hop but duplicates selection logic in clients and may rely on stale caches. A server-side strategy centralises routing and cross-cutting controls but introduces proxy capacity, configuration and failure concerns.

Neither architecture guarantees an even CPU load. A round-robin rule balances **request counts**, not necessarily work. If one request takes a second and another takes a millisecond, identical counts can imply very different utilisation.

## Make the policy measurable

Measure successful request rate, latency, failure rate, current in-flight work, instance saturation and distribution per endpoint. Determine whether retries could accidentally amplify traffic to a struggling node.

## The lab

Order keeps a two-item list of Product URLs and advances an index after each order attempt:

~~~js
const target = productInstances[nextProduct++ % productInstances.length];
~~~

This is the smallest possible example of **client-side round robin**. It is not service discovery and does not automatically remove a failed endpoint.

## Challenge

If Product A becomes slow but keeps returning 200, will round robin protect Order? Not by itself. You still need deadlines, optional health-aware selection, and resilience controls.

## Test your reasoning

Name the component that owns this responsibility, explain its behaviour during a failure, and identify one configuration or metric you would verify in production.
